A toss is a quick, light, often casual motion — either of throwing something, moving something suddenly, or flipping something. The word captures the idea of something being sent through the air without much force, or something moving in a brief, sharp way.

When you throw something in a relaxed, easy, short-ranged way — not hard, not carefully aimed, just a simple fling — that single act of throwing is called a toss.

  • "She caught the keys after a perfect toss across the room."
  • "With one toss, the paper ball landed straight in the bin."
  • "Give me a toss of the pen, will you?"

The key idea here is easiness and lightness. A toss is never a powerful throw or a long throw. It's something you do without much effort, usually over a short distance. You wouldn't describe a baseball pitcher's throw as a toss — that would be too powerful. But throwing something to someone sitting nearby? That's a toss.
Meaning 2: A Coin Flip (The Most Common Use)

This is probably the meaning you'll encounter most often. A toss refers to the act of flipping a coin in the air to make a random decision. The coin spins, lands, and the result — heads or tails — decides something. Because the outcome is left to pure chance, a "toss" here represents fairness and randomness.

  • "They decided who goes first by a toss."
  • "India won the toss and chose to bat."
  • "Let's settle this with a toss."

This meaning is especially important in sports. In cricket, football, and tennis, captains or players "win the toss" or "lose the toss" at the start of a match. Winning the toss gives you the advantage of choosing — for example, in cricket, you decide whether to bat or bowl first.

You'll also hear the phrase "coin toss", which simply makes the coin part explicit. It means exactly the same thing.
Meaning 3: A Sharp Movement of the Head

A toss can describe a quick, sudden upward or sideways movement of the head. This motion is usually a physical expression of an emotion — pride, dismissal, irritation, attitude, or even just moving hair out of the face. You'll almost always see this in the phrase "a toss of the head" or "with a toss of her head."

  • "With a toss of her head, she walked away without saying a word."
  • "He gave a toss of his head to show he wasn't interested."
  • "She tossed her head — a toss that said everything without speaking."

Think of it as a gesture. The head jerks back, or flicks to one side, briefly and sharply. It's a very vivid image, and writers use it often to show a character's attitude or mood without having to explain it in words.

In cooking, a toss refers to the action of mixing ingredients by lifting and turning them, usually in a bowl or pan. When you "toss a salad," you're lifting the leaves and other ingredients and turning them so the dressing coats everything evenly.

  • "Give the salad a good toss before serving."
  • "The pasta just needs a quick toss in the sauce."
  • "A toss in the pan for thirty seconds and it's ready."

The word "toss" is used here because the action looks a little like throwing — you're lifting ingredients and letting them fall back down loosely, not stirring them in circles. In kitchens, this is a standard technique, and you'll hear it very frequently in cooking instructions.

In British English, a toss appears in the very common informal phrase "not give a toss," which means to not care at all about something. This is a slightly blunt, casual way of expressing complete indifference.

  • "I don't give a toss what they think of me."
  • "He didn't give a single toss about the meeting."
  • "She couldn't give a toss whether they agreed or not."

You may also hear "couldn't give a toss" — same meaning. This phrase is very natural in everyday British speech and not considered strongly offensive, though it is informal. If you're watching British films, TV shows, or reading British fiction, you'll come across it regularly.

Because a coin toss is 50-50, the word toss has extended to describe any situation where two outcomes are equally likely — where you genuinely can't predict which will happen.

  • "It's a toss between the two of them — either could win."
  • "Getting there on time is a toss — it depends entirely on traffic."

The compound form "toss-up" is far more commonly used for this meaning, but you will occasionally see the single word "toss" used this way too.
How to Tell the Meanings Apart in Context

Since "toss" has several meanings, the surrounding words will almost always make it clear:

  • "Win/lose the toss," "decide by a toss," "coin toss" → it's about flipping a coin.
  • "A toss of the head," "with a toss of her/his head" → it's the head movement.
  • "Give it a toss," "needs a toss" in a cooking context → it's about mixing food.
  • "Not give a toss," "couldn't give a toss" → it's the British expression for not caring.
  • A throw described as easy and short-ranged → it's the basic meaning of a light throw.
  • "It's a toss between X and Y" → it means an equally balanced, unpredictable choice.

All these meanings share the same underlying spirit: something quick, light, and somewhat casual. Whether it's a lazy throw, a coin spinning in the air, a sharp flick of the head, or a quick mix of salad — a "toss" always implies something brief and easy, never heavy or laboured. Once you hold that image, every use of this word will feel natural and intuitive.
